title: SpaceX Targets Late 2026 for First Starship Orbital Flight After Record IPO
excerpt: Elon Musk tells shareholders the company aims to launch and catch its next Starship this month, as Falcon 9 bookings dry up through 2029.
body:
• SpaceX is targeting late 2026 for Starship's first orbital mission, which will deploy next-generation Starlink satellites — a milestone after 13 suborbital test flights.
  • CEO Elon Musk confirmed during his first earnings call since SpaceX's June IPO that the company aims to launch and catch the next Starship this month.
  • Falcon 9 is fully booked until 2028-2029, with Starlink missions now consuming 79% of SpaceX's launch manifest, up from 54% in 2020.
  • SpaceX's longer-term plans include orbital AI data centres and a lunar lander for NASA's Artemis programme, with dozens of in-space refuelling tests required.

SpaceX has confirmed plans to begin orbital flights of its Starship rocket by late 2026, a landmark transition from the suborbital test programme that has defined the world's largest rocket since its maiden launch in April 2023.

The announcement came as CEO Elon Musk addressed investors in his first earnings call since SpaceX went public in June, telling shareholders the company intends to launch and catch its next Starship as soon as this month. The planned flight would mark the 14th overall test of the Starship-Super Heavy system.

From Suborbital Tests to Orbit

All 13 previous Starship test flights followed suborbital trajectories, with the upper stage splashing down — or intended to splash down — in the Indian Ocean. The shift to orbital missions represents a fundamental change in the programme's objectives.

https://x.com/SpaceX/status/2084737174709403899

The first orbital flights are expected to carry larger Starlink satellites and test in-space propellant transfer, a capability critical to the lunar lander version of Starship being developed for NASA's Artemis programme. NASA's contract with SpaceX involves dozens of in-space refuelling flights and tests, with the moon lander targeted for use as soon as 2028.

SpaceX's most recent flight, the 13th, launched from its Starbase headquarters in South Texas in late July. It was the second flight using the upgraded Version 3 hardware, which includes more powerful Raptor 3 engines and an upgraded payload dispenser.

A Rocket Company That Became a Satellite Giant

The push toward orbital flights is driven in part by SpaceX's own demand for launch capacity. Starlink, the company's satellite internet constellation, brought in $11.4 billion in revenue in 2025 — roughly 60% of SpaceX's total — and has deployed more than 10,000 satellites to date.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=OPfT8wu-0FA

That internal demand is squeezing out external customers. Starlink's share of SpaceX's Falcon 9 missions has risen from 54% in 2020 to about 79% so far in 2026, according to a Reuters analysis. At least seven spacecraft companies have been told Falcon 9 is fully booked until 2028 or 2029.

"SpaceX has a scarce resource, which is their own launch capacity. If they were to use the same launch capacity for an external customer, they are giving up the profits they could have earned by flying their own internal satellites."

— Akhil Rao, Chief Economist, Rational Futures

Orbital AI Data Centres

SpaceX has disclosed plans to use Starship to launch up to one million solar-powered satellites engineered as orbital AI data centres. The company stated in its IPO prospectus that it "may prioritise our own launch payloads over additional U.S. government contracts or third-party customers."

The ambition has sent tremors through the commercial launch industry. Falcon 9 prices have risen from around $54 million in 2013 to roughly $74 million today, and analysts warn that a vertically integrated SpaceX could further raise the cost of space access for competitors.

Competitors Under Pressure

SpaceX's dominance faces limited near-term challengers. Blue Origin's New Glenn rocket exploded on a launchpad in May and will be grounded at least until year's end. United Launch Alliance's Vulcan rocket has been grounded since February over a booster issue. Rocket Lab, which is second to SpaceX in launch rate, is developing a reusable rocket called Neutron and is in the process of acquiring satellite communications firm Iridium for $8 billion.

What's Next

If this month's flight test succeeds, SpaceX will move closer to demonstrating the full reusability that underpins Starship's economic case — catching the Super Heavy booster on the launch tower rather than discarding it. The orbital missions that follow later this year will determine whether Starship can meet its commercial and government commitments, from deploying next-generation Starlink satellites to supporting NASA's return to the Moon.
